utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Please be seated. Anything to be discussed before the witness enters the courtroom? The Defence is prepared to show the witness his name that we have it as evidence, then let us hear the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian with Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the usher to escort the witness in the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. You can hear me in a language you understand, Witness DA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We can proceed, and the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would first like and ask the usher to show the witness his name so he can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please tell us if it is your name on this sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, yes. It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Can this be marked an exhibit for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. DA, can we resume?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the interpreters hear the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, they can, although they have a lot of noise in their headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Can we proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's try.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Witness DA, yesterday, we broke off at the time when you were describing to us how you had been beaten and how a neighbour of yours had saved your life. What happened after the 22nd of April, 1992? Did you -- were you mobilised in some way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must ask you for something because -- for a correction. Before the 22nd of April, can I tell you what happened on the 26th of May -- March, excuse me. May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned from the prison for the second time, on the 26th of March, 1992, the Croatian forces crossed -- that is, the Sava River near Sijekovac where the population is mixed. Muslims, Croats, Serbs. And with the HVO's help, that is, with the help of Bosnian Muslims and Croats, they surrounded that village and butchered the civilian population. Over 20 civilians were slain on their doorsteps, and I am sure that other witnesses will be able to tell you more about it because they had gone through that and survived that. The media in Bosanski Brod reported that those were Chetniks, that all the slain people were Chetniks. So that on the 27th of March, 1992, the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina headed by Mr. Fikret Abdic, Franjo Boras, Mr., and Mrs. Biljana Plavsic came to visit that village, and saw on the spot and saw with their own eyes the scale of the massacre committed there, over innocent civilians, children, and old people. Television Sarajevo, Sarajevo television and Jutel television covered that event, but it was then and never again. After that, representatives of religious communities came, Bishop Kacavenda, Archbishop of Zvornik and Tuzla, Archbishop Vinko Puljic, Reso Elimar [phoen], Jusuf Jakubovski [phoen], that is Selimovski, I'm sorry, Selimovski, to try to calm down the tension. However, it did not help. The fighting went on. There was fighting in the direction of Serb villages, and what happened after that, we who were blocked in the town, in Bosanski Brod, the military command ordered all of us to report to certain places. And I did that. My meeting point was the Unema [phoen] Warehouse. We reported there. Our names were taken down. We were about 350, I think. I mean, I'm just making a guess, but I believe we were 350. Around 350. We were told that we had to turn up every morning at 7.00 for the lineup, and we were used as labour, for the hardest types of manual labour. And as the front was advancing towards Serb villages, we were ordered to dig trenches along the frontlines for the Croatian army so that a number of inmates were killed, and there are documents to attest to that, as they dug the trenches on the frontline.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know something about the attack on the village of Lijeska, and do you personally have anything to do with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As the front was advancing towards Serb villages, they took us by night. They made us climb up on to the flat roofs to look how Serb houses were burning, and that was sheer horror. I mean, you know where your brother's, your parents' house are, where somebody else's houses are. And you see them ablaze and you don't know what is happening. The troops were pulling out, and the civilians were also withdrawing with them. In that village you were asking me about, my father had stayed behind there. He was 85 years old at the time. I'm sorry. He had been bedridden for five years. His grandchildren are both Serbs and Croats. The Croatian army, the 108th, found him in the house. He was shot dead, and he burned together with his house. An old man, 85, ill, treated in Slavonski Brod five times, underwent surgery three times, and he wrote about him that he was a Chetnik. And thus eliminated him in the most brutal way imaginable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we go on, Mr. DA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Until when were you under the labour obligation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order to report to the army command was issued sometime in the early days of May, or late April. I can't remember the exact date. But this order exists. I stayed there until the beginning of September. I was a member of this labour brigade. But let's make things clear. It was called a labour brigade, but it was a camp. Let me just tell you this briefly in two sentences. We had no food. They did not treat us as human beings, but as livestock, as beasts. There was nowhere to wash. There was no toilet. We tried to somehow make do when we worked out in the fields. We pulled out some roots, that is, carrots, potatoes, onions. We had to hide them because that was the only food that we had. And a soldier guarding us, even Brizic's son, if he found a carrot hidden somewhere on our bodies, then such a person remembered well, the son of Ivan Brizic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you beaten as you worked there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every morning when we would line up, Ivan Brizic's son, I do not know his name, but I know the dad very well, he had a whip and beat us in circles. It was the place for physical culture, and he used this whip to beat us. I still have marks, scars, on my head because my skin had split. We had absolutely no health care, feverish, full in wounds [as interpreted] without the change of clothes. Unwashed, unfed. That is what our life was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did any of the inmates die when -- during the digging of the trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember his name, but one can find it in documents, there is also their order establishing the death of an inmate during the trench digging. And may I also add that it was terribly difficult it -- better description.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I would like the usher to show the witness a document. Your Honour, those documents are not translated. They are on our list, and they have been submitted for the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the interpreters do not have the copies at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. May I just interrupt. First, the Prosecution wanted to take the floor. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Normally Your Honour, we show the exhibit to the other side before it's presented to the witness. And we never received copies of this, it's hard to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We also would prefer to see the documents first. And then may they be copied for the translation booth. Maybe Defence counsel can proceed with other questions when they are copied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just state our position on this. For this week and these witnesses, we have no objection to doing it whatever way is most convenient for the Defence because of our general position about the relevance of this testimony. But we hope that when we get to other witnesses in the future, that we will have exhibits before the witness testifies translated so that we can take a position on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There is no doubt --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have copies for Your Honours and for the Registrar here, only they are not translated so that's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you could please present them to the translation booths.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Just give me one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May these documents be marked provisionally D31, the one dated 14th of June, 1992. And the other dated 10 August 1992, D32. But we decide as usual only on the admission of these in evidence after we have heard the translation. May we ask the witness to be so kind and read out these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I to stand up?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, sit down.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "HVO, the command of the 102nd Bosnian Brigade, Municipality of Odzak."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just go on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Number 153/92".

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters still do not have copies of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "On the 14th of June, 1992 --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you to stop for a moment. The photocopies have not yet arrived with the booths. It's the usher's first day in the courtroom. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, does counsel have extra copies for the Court and for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have only one extra copy for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can start, Mr. DA, with this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have the copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "At your request, number 13/8/01/95/3292 we hereby prove to the public security station to take an inmate from the military prison, Goran Panic and Mladin Sumar from Brusnica. The detainees are taken in order to clear the mine fields in Gornji Svilaj. Upon the completion of this task, the inmates shall be returned to the military prison. The inmates should be handed over against the appropriate documentation. Made in four copies. Sent to. Written by, initials AM/OG. Sent to the public security station, the military police, the military prison, and a copy for the files. Ivica Matanovic, commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please turn the page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can please the counsel switch on his microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The Republic of Croatia, the command of the SAM/MOT battalion, number 81/92/01. File number 1099/01/92/93. Novo Selo, 10 August 1992. To the military police of the 101st Bosanski Brod Brigade, the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Brod Municipality: Report on 9 August, 1992, at 10.30. While digging trenches on the reserve frontline, Spasoje Krsic was killed by a mortar shell. 68th battalion of the military police, the 3rd detachment of the independent motorised battery commandant of the independent motorised battery, Zdravko Lukanovic, stamped." Yes, these are confirmations that the inmates were taken to dig trenches, and that they were killed while digging trenches unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness DA, for reading out these provisionally marked documents as 31, 32. Objections by the Prosecutions to the authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask ex officio the Defence, is this the best possible copy available or do you have the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, we can ask the witness because he provided these documents to us. He is the head of some organisation, and they collected those documents. He can maybe explain how he got those documents. And if I may, I can ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so before we decide on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Witness DA, did you see these documents before? How did you come by these documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to documents, after the fall of Bosanski Brod and Odzak, when the Serbs returned those territories, the Croatian army left these documents behind, not only these documents, there are more of them. We have collected these documents, and we are in their possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you maybe have the original of this document? Can you maybe check whether you have it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that for a fact, but this is a photocopy of the document, so this means that the original should exist. The evidence has remained, the original evidence has remained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. These documents are admitted into evidence as D31, D32 respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] If I may ask the usher, sorry, to show the witness the next document. This is for the translation booth, for the Chambers, for the witness, and for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please put your glasses on, Mr. DA, because I'm going to ask you to read this document as well. Please start reading, and if you can do it a bit faster.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I? "HVO, the command of the 102 Brigade, Bosanska Posivina, number 61/92, the 28th of May, 1992. The order for the chief of medical staff and the commander of the military prison. 1, it is hereby ordered to the chief of the medical staff to carry out the medical examination and to provide medical care for the following inmates: One, Alexander Stanisic. Two, Oliver Ostojic. Three, Dusan Vijic, who are currently in the Strolit prison. The commander of the prison is hereby ordered to provide better food, warmer clothes for the aforementioned inmates, and to discontinue any physical ill treatment. The aforementioned measures are undertaken because these inmates are being prepared for exchange. Sent to the chief of the medical staff, to the commander of the military post, the commander of the prison. For the files. Commander, Ivica Matanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any objections, especially to the authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, D33.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I would like the usher to distribute the next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask Defence counsel how long do you intend to proceed? Yesterday you announced that you would need another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When we made our plan for the examination of these witness, we had in mind that we have to finish on Wednesday. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it was clear enough yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll try our best to finish in the next 15, 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you again please put your glasses on. You don't have to read the names. Can you please just describe this document to us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a list for the exchange of women and children. The list contains the names of 50 women and 50 children. The list was prepared for the exchange on the 4th of July, 1992, in the Odzak school camp. My question here is, what international law says that women and children may be prisoners of war? And these women and children were in our group.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you find this together with other documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... in evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections as to authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, D34.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please start reading this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "To the command of the rear echelon, Bosanski Brod Sijekovac, to whom it may concern: It is hereby confirmed that the intervention platoon for Zagreb has the right to bring in the following females: Andja Novakovic, and Petra Nisic, on behalf of the males. The persons should be brought in at 1800 hours. These persons will sleep in the basement of the facility. In case they resist, you are allowed to use force. Commander Ahmet Causevic." And the second document: "To the command of the rear echelon, Sijekovac, Bosanski Brod, to whom it may concern: It is hereby confirmed that the intervention platoon from Sijekovac may bring in the following females, Dragica Mijatovic and Grozda Petrovic on behalf of the males. The persons will be brought in in the evening, and they will be released to their homes in the morning. The persons will spend the night in the basement. In case of resistance, you are allowed to use force. Commander, Ahmet Causevic." And I'm sure that other witnesses will describe what happened. It is their document again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Can this be marked, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objections today to any of the documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, D35.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the name of the organisation that you have founded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an association of prisoners of war and inmates of Srpski Bosanski Brod. It is a nongovernmental organisation, nonpartisan organisation, and its members are all those who were imprisoned in the camps in Bosanski Brod. And there were over ten of them. Over 2.000 women, children, and elderly people were incarcerated in the camps in Bosanski Brod. I must say that many have died taking the truth with them to their graves. 21 inmates from only one village have died so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have also compiled some documents in that organisation of yours. I'm going to show you the documents. You don't have to read them. Can you just confirm for the Chamber how these documents were compiled, and whether they are truthful to the best of your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Could the usher distribute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document on which it says "Annex, 9.14," and starting with page 4, it contains photographs. What does this document describe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was compiled based on authentic statements by the families of the civilians, Muslims, Serbs, and Croats, who have perished. So this is an authentic document on the suffering of the civilians in Sijekovac. Among whom there were also Muslims, Mustafa Kovacevic, Mustafa Alic. There are also Croats. Ivan Rudes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know why these Muslims and Croats were killed? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mustafa Kovacevic and the other Kovacevic were killed because they helped the Serbs to remain alive, not to be killed. And that was the only reason why they were killed. At the time, in 1992, helping a Serb and a member of the orthodox religion to stay alive by any Croat equalled an act of heroism. And because they helped the innocent people, they were killed by their own. Gentlemen, here you can see on page 11 the one photo but last is the photo of my father, 85 years of age my father was. He has more Croat grandchildren than Serb grandchildren, but still he was slain in the most atrocious way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, can this exhibit be marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, D36.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document which shows -- which says "Annex 1.17" on page 1, what this document about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was compiled by us, and it speaks of a group of recruits, members of the Yugoslav People's Army, who came as young men who had just joined the army to complete their compulsory military service. So the first days of their army service were in Bosanski Brod. They were not trained, and they were captured in the Koliba sector. They were brought in. Among them was the father of a recruit who had come to save his son from that army. Here is the evidence proving that these soldiers, these recruits, were alive when they were captured by the Croatian army. Those who were of Croat, Albanian, and Muslim ethnic background were sent home. And the lot of the others is not known until this very day. Until Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this very day, it is not known where the father of this recruit is. His destiny is also unknown. The Croatian authorities were asked to tell us where the graves of these young men are; however, they do not admit anything. There is, however, a videotape showing these young men with their arms in the air. That showed that they surrendered, but their lot is not known. It is not known until this very day where their graves are. A mass grave is being dug up these days in Slavonski Brod, so we assume that their remains may be found there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Witness DA, may I ask you, here we can read "Annex 1.17." Annex to what, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is an annex to the criminal report for genocide and aggression on the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the Croatian army, and that crime was committed on the 3rd of March, 1992, and that is when the war started in Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the 3rd of March, 1992, in Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And this was compiled by your nongovernmental organisation, too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is a nongovernmental organisation, and the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Can this be marked, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's a little bit difficult because normally we don't admit an annex without having the entire document. Maybe it's only to be understood in the entire context, but under the present circumstances, it is admitted into evidence as number D37.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we may provide you with the main document as well. But on that document, there are basically only the names of the persons who committed those crimes. So I don't know if you are interested in having that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it might be interesting for the Prosecution if they don't have this document already for the alleged crimes committed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They do have all those documents and the main document, Your Honour. It has been submitted to them, I guess, a year ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we are distributing the next document, can you tell us who was in power in Bosanski Brod as of the 3rd of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of the 3rd of March, 1992, the power in Bosanski Brod was held by the military. The HDZ and the SDA had played a major part in that. The military -- there were very many changes in this military government. The first one was Mirko Jelinic. And then some people from Zagreb came and replaced him. The so-called HOS. Then they brought in Mr. Gahic. Then Ivan Brizic was also there so that they changed people in responsible positions, but it was by and large the military rule under the command and the jurisdiction of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the Serbs in Bosanski Brod, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a definitive answer whether they were or were not armed, but I can tell you about an incident --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But be brief, because we are coming to an end.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Tuzla Corps was made of Croats, Muslims, Albanians, and Serbs. Propaganda originating with the Croatian army was very powerful so that the young men were fleeing from that corps and joining the Croatian army. They were casting away their weapons, and that is why this corps withdrew from Bosanski Brod. The corps was joined by Serb volunteers. They took up arms and joined that corps. It is common fact that pilots also deserted the Yugoslav army. Whoever was of Croat or Muslim ethnic background deserted that army, and that was the upshot of the propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know, have you heard, where did you go when they left the JNA, its members of Croat and Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw with my own eyes when I was on the bridge. They immediately took off the caps of their heads and they discarded their weapons into the Sava, and immediately as they crossed the bridge they joined the ZNG. Some people who were sick or not up to the standard were sent to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness DA.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel has used the last name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the end of the examination-in-chief, but perhaps the Prosecution or Their Honours will have some questions for you. So please, remain where you are. [In English] If possible to strike from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You tendered --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And if the last exhibit could be marked, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, my question. Admitted into evidence, D38. Could the registry please take care of that last name be redacted. And then for the cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask the usher to move the ELMO so that I have a line of sight to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Witness DA, excuse me if I do not call you Witness DA. That will confuse me because in my language, DA is the Prosecutor. And I know that (redacted). But I will call you, so that the record is clear, "sir" or "witness." Witness, sir, thank you for coming today. And thank you for telling us about the crimes that you witnessed, and thank you for your work in documenting crimes that happened in Bosnia. Can you tell the Judges why it is so important that a record be kept and that the truth be known about crimes and war crimes committed against innocent civilians in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. It is important, and how. It is important to tell the truth before this Honourable Court. If the Court is here to provide fair trial, then it needs to hear the truth. The truth must be told, and the truth must be the starting point because there can be no reconciliation in Bosnia until all sides to what happened tell their own truth. Things will not calm down in Bosnia until all the sides tell their truth, and then we shall be able to forgive one another, and then we shall be able to live together. Whoever denies the truth, he is causing trouble also to the European Community and to his or her own people. And that is why we founded our association, so that the truth could be heard of any ethnic group because every victim has its own executioner, and every executioner has a first and a last name. Whatever his ethnic background may be or his faith may be, he should be brought to account before this Court, and that is what we are fighting for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And you yourself, sir, from what you've told us of your background, experienced many things and lived your life in a community that was mixed of ethnicities, and your own family was mixed with Croats, with, in fact, the people that perpetrated these crimes, or many of these crimes, the ethnic group in Bosanski Brod. Isn't that correct? You were married to a Croat, and you had children that you considered your children, who were of Croatian descent. Correct? Stepchildren?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. In my family, you said a sentence which was not all right, that you said there were those who had committed something. But nobody from my family has committed any wrong deed. So let us be clear about that. The two of us, my wife and I, cannot be blamed, cannot be held responsible for the disintegration of Yugoslavia. There are two factors which are to blame, one is external and the other one is internal. I do not wish to speak about the external factor. It is up to history to tell, that but what I am referring to is the internal factor. And that is, and I want Their honours to hear that, that as long as we have chauvinistic parties in power which brandish emblems and symbols about what happened during World War II, as long as they brandish Hitler symbols, there can be no peace. And we must do our utmost that every -- representatives of every people explain to their own people what has happened because what was happened now in the Netherlands if somebody picked up the flag with Swastikas going around, of course there would be a reaction and that is what is happening in our case. Once people understand that, that is our problem. That is when this particular problem will be solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned that in fact when you were arrested and abused that they referred to you as a Chetnik. And believe me, sir, I am not at all saying that that's true. What I'd like you to explain that isn't it a fact that those who perpetrated the crimes and those who incited the crimes brought up these symbols labelling all Serbs "Chetniks," labelling all Croats "Ustasha," calling Muslims "balijas" or "mujahedin," and that these kinds of misuse of history helped incite the crimes that were committed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, you who did not participate in it, of course, have difficulty in understanding the evil that happened or to understand the Balkan mindset. What happened in our case, what is still happening, what happened in Kosovo, Albanians are not to blame, Croats are not to blame, Serbs are not to blame. It is a virus which has somehow been sewn amongst those people to sew strife. And this comes through religious communities, through existing on nationalism on chauvinism in whatever European country somebody starts, existing on nationalism, there will be trouble. We never thought about that. My late father took care of in the same way of a child of Croat background and a Serb background, and more of his grandchildren were of predominantly Croat background than of predominantly Serb background. And nonetheless, he lost his life in a very cruel way even though he was innocent. And I am still suffering today. I have been suffering for more than ten years because a state may fall apart. You may lose your state. You lose your home but when you lose your family members, then you are reduced to nothing. When you lose your next of kin, and I've lost mine because they are on two sides. Some are in Croatia and some are now in Bosnia, in Republika Srpska, and it is very difficult to live with that. And let me just add that the mixed marriages suffer the most. I think we fared the worst and we are still the chief victims because as long as we have the jingoistic parties in power, children of mixed marriages and children from such marriages will be the chief victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, we haven't -- Bosanski Brod has not really been the subject of this trial, so we don't know a lot about it. But let me just get some basic facts from you. Bosanski Brod is on the Sava River, and in fact it was very close to the fighting in Croatia in 1991, the Tuzla Corps of the JNA had troops stationed, is that correct, in Bosanski Brod? I see you shaking your head, so correct me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to correct you. Oh, dear. You have to understand that this Court will not be able to pass a fair judgement until the Court understands who started it first. The war started with the secession of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. republics --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to stop you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the war started in Croatia, in Croatia, on the 4th or the 5th of May, 1991 when Bijelis, which was a Serb municipality, was attacked in Slavonski Brod. On the 15th of July, it was attacked for the second time, and 87 Serbs were taken to camps and prisons. On the 21st to the 22nd July, 1991, I had my summer cottage in Croatia. It was looted and put fire to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of September -- on the 16th of September, from Croatia, fire was opened on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is on Serb villages. And on the 16th of September, Endenija [phoen] Goranovic whilst at his workplace because a shell had been fired from Slavonski Brod. So the Croatia carried the war from its territory into the Bosnia-Herzegovina territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you have to limit -- you're an attorney. I think you know this -- your answers to the particular question that I ask because I know that you have a lot of knowledge about events that you could share with us, but we are limited in time. Is it correct that Bosanski Brod is located on the Sava River bordering Croatia? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Before the war, Bosanski Brod had a mixed population. About 40 per cent were Croat, about 31 per cent were of Serb -- identified themselves as Serbs, and about 13 per cent identified themselves as Muslim. Would that approximately correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that your data are accurate because you are missing Yugoslavs. And about 8.000 citizens there were people who declared themselves as Yugoslavs. Those were mostly the mixed marriages, so when you have this information and then you would have different ratios. But what I have to say also to this Court, between the Bosnian and -- between the Bosanski and Slavonski Brod there is the River Sava, and there is a bridge. And there was a slogan on that bridge. "Forbidden to Serbs and dogs."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you go from Bosanski Brod, if you want to cross to the Croatian side, then dogs and Serbs were prohibited from going over there, so what does that tell you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, can you try to limit your answers to the questions I ask. What you're saying may be important, but both attorneys will have a chance to ask you questions. You talked in your testimony, you told us about many experiences that you had, where in fact you were saved by people of Croatian descent, individuals. You talked about a soldier, I believe, yesterday who called your wife when you were first held in the prison. You talked about another soldier that gave you a ride, I believe, to your house, remembered you as being an attorney who had helped him on a case. And you talked about a woman who risked her life to save you when someone was trying to slit your throat. All of these were Croats. Correct? Is that yes, sir? I'm sorry, you have to answer outloud.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have nothing against Croats. They are very nice people. But you have to understand, you have to understand, that the nationalist, the chauvinists played the role. Not all the Serbs are Chetniks, not all the Croats are Ustasha, not all the Muslims are mujahedin. But the faith played a part in this because the ethnic background -- the faith, the religion played its part because they were the ones who infiltrated those slogans, those things. When after Tudjman -- when they said you decide about Croatia, but who is in Croatia in who lived in Croatia? Why did they on the 22nd of September, 1992, why did they say the Serb people were not longer a constituent people of Croatia. Why did they include in their constitution the emblems dating back to World War II. That is what caused the rebellion, and that I think was something that somebody was trying to stir up we and that is what brought down Yugoslavia because we all lived well. We all got along well, but somebody put a bone of contention between us. I mean, I meet Croats here, and we hug each other because it is not his fault that he had been misled. And until we managed to do away with this form of deception of people, of -- because in the Netherlands, I mean, you don't have only Dutch, there are all sorts of people here. And yet you all get along well. And somebody wants to pit us against each other because they know how we slaughtered one another in World War II. And I know what that was like. But this one was much worse. It was much more lethal, and there was no rule, international law, which could describe this one because they tortured in 147 different ways. And when I'm saying this, I'm not referring to the Croat people. I'm not referring to the Muslim people because it has nothing to do with peoples. I'm talking about extremists in every one of those peoples. And there are also extremists in my people, and they also need to be brought to account here, and the same yardstick has to be applied to all of them, and hence our association.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I think everyone in the courtroom agrees with you about that. Sir, in Bosanski Brod today -- let me go back. Would it be correct that the Croatian army occupied Bosanski Brod until, and you can correct me about the date, I believe it was sometime in 1993 when at the same time that the Croatian army withdrew from northern Bosnia, JNA and Montenegrin units withdrew from areas of south of Dubrovnik, that these two events occurred together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say. And let me just correct you a little. On the 3rd of March, Croatia attacked Bosnia and Herzegovina in Bosanski Brod. They forced the Sava River and its units, entered Bosanski Brod and villages with Croat population. So this was logistics together with Croats and Muslims who agreed with what they were doing. They attacked Serb villages, and Posavina is a scorched land. Only one house of 3500, only one house, and its number is 108, only that one remained unscathed. All the others were burned down. My house was burned down. I lost my house. The Tuzla Corps fell apart because it was mixed. Because there were Croats and Muslims and Serbs, so that it broke down. And as the corps pulled out, the Serb people also withdrew with them. On the 7th of October, the Serb people organised -- the 7th of October, 1992, I'm saying, they took back Bosanski Brod. They took back Bosanski Brod again. When people arrived on the spot, and when they could see the Serb religious facilities, houses of worship, churches, cemeteries had been burned down or damaged, monuments dating to World War II also damaged and destroyed, then Serb defenders also engaged in vandalism, and they destroyed a mosque. That was the end of 1992. In early 1992, that is, in March, because in Bosanski Brod, on the 5th of July at 5.00, 1992, the Serb church was mined. And it was built more than 150 years ago. When that church was mined, I and a few more prominent citizens were brought there to take out the icons because a Croat tank was -- tanker was to bring -- Croats' tank was to come there. I cannot tell you about Dubrovnik and the second fall of Brod because I am not aware of that. But what I am aware, I know what I am telling you about now because I brought these documents, and the Honourable Court has those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know in Bosanski Brod at the end of the war, the time of Dayton, what was the population, the ethnic mix of the population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs became the predominant group because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'll ask you because, in fact, it was virtually Serb. Almost all the Croats and Muslims left except for a handful. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no. May I ask you a question in turn? What is the ethnic composition of Croatia? What was it at that time and what is it now? Isn't Europe ashamed to have a purely Catholic state in its midst? 560.000 Serbs were expelled from Croatia. They still cannot go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosanski Brod, in Bosanski Brod, in 1992, there were Croats, Croat men and Croat women, Muslim men and Muslim women. They were not ill treated. The Serbs did not set up camps for them, did not put them in camps and torture them as those others did in the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, you're not answering my question. You're a lawyer, you know that in a courtroom, to get -- so we can reach the end and finish we need you to answers the questions that are asked. We're not trying to debate and I'm not trying to debate with you. All of your points may be valid, but here we're here to answer the questions that are asked. The Judges may have some questions for you later. The question was, what was the composition, if you know - if you don't know, say so - of Bosanski Brod at the time of the Dayton accords?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no census, and therefore I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir. You lived there, and you saw the events that happened in Bosanski Brod. Would you agree with me that everyone who lived in that town would have seen what the Croatian army was doing? That all of the people, including the leadership that the Croats put into the civilian government were aware of the massive crimes that were going on against Serb civilians in Bosanski Brod in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, sir: These Croats, Croats who committed those crimes that I told you about, and other witnesses to this day, they still walk around this Bosanski Brod and nobody is arresting them. And that is what irks people there. Because wrongdoers must be removed from amongst the other citizens so that people can come to terms with what happened, reconcile, and go back to normal life again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I want to get to that, but first I'd like you to answer the questions that I ask you. The question was that isn't it correct that in 1992 in Bosanski Brod, you talked about that in Posavina, house after house was burned to the ground? Everyone who lived there was aware that massive crime going on against the Serb civilians, including the Croatian civilian leadership were aware of the crimes going on against Serb civilians in the camps. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They issued such orders, and they knew. And to this day, they walk around Bosanski Brod and nobody asks them any questions. We meet. He fetches up in front of me, and he hugs me. Gives me a kiss now. And in 1992, when he beat me, I was a Chetnik to him and I can forgive him that because we have to forgive such things. But let everybody account for what he did, if he beat me, so let him account for beating me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: One other point: You talked about people who were massacred, whose bodies are still missing, whose graves have never been discovered. Can you tell the Court why it's important in your community and to the people who come from where you live to find the bodies of their loved ones who were killed and dumped into mass graves or hidden from view and whose bodies have to this day not yet been discovered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very difficult question. A major problem, too. On the 6th and on the 7th of September of this year, we had a joint meeting of the associations of Croatia, Slavonia, Zagreb, Belgrade, Sarajevo, the federation, Republika Srpska, and the meeting took place in Bosanski Brod. And we addressed this issue, and we begged everybody concerned where the graves of the missing civilians are so that the mothers, the sisters, the fathers can at least light a candle at the place where their Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. loved ones are buried. This was a good meeting, fortunately. And there are results. And the mass grave which was discovered in Slavonski Brod after this meeting, we were told that there were five graves there, and digging is underway. And when the first grave was dug up and was marked by NN, we found 11 dead bodies there. And that was also the case in the next one, and in the following one. And there is another mass grave above them which is still closed. We didn't know of its existence before this meeting. So let's sober up and let us say to each other where the mass graves are so that we can all find our loved ones in order to be able to light a candle where they were buried. And this is the only way how people can be reconciled, how people can forgive each other. When we find the graves of our loved ones. It is terrible when a mother doesn't know where her son is. And I'm sure that we will hear from the witnesses who are looking for their three brothers, for their fathers, and they don't know where their graves are. For Europe to be able to reign in the Balkans, we have to deal with this preliminary question in a sincere way. Once this is done, once we forgive each other, then there will be no problems. We are good people. We are diligent people. We will be reconciled. We only have to do away with the chauvinist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The trial stays adjourned until 11.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, I have only three questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's appropriate if you can include this in the line of questions emanating from the line of questions put forward by the Judges. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Following the line of questions we just heard, I think as Prosecution counsel correctly pointed out, everybody in this courtroom will share your view that there is not only one responsible party, that there is a number of responsibles from all groups unfortunately [Realtime transcript read in error "fortunately"] deciding to go -- to proceed on an avenue which only can be called criminal behaviour. And it's for this Tribunal to prosecute and to take the necessary consequences against whomsoever from which ethnic group soever. I only wanted to ask you the following question: In agreement with nearly all the witnesses we heard here, it was testified that before, let's call it neutral, the events happened in 1991, 1992, following years, the ethnic groups lived together peacefully in Former Yugoslavia. What would be from your point of view the exact date or the approximate date since when this destruction of the peaceful living-together of all ethnical or religious groups started? And where do you see the reasons for this development?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people of the Former Yugoslavia, as you said it yourself, lived in a community, in a state which had its constitution, its joint army, and its joint organs. The 14th congress of the league of communists of the Former Yugoslavia which took place in 1990 meant the break out of that party and that was also the beginning of the disintegration of Yugoslavia. Two factors influenced those developments. There was an external factor and an internal factor. I cannot talk about the external factor. It's up to history to talk about that. As for the internal factors, I've already said something. All the republics in the Former Yugoslavia were states, virtual states. They had their territory and all the other characteristics of states. And this is the origin of all the evil. The republics which wanted to secede from the Former Yugoslavia, but instead of doing it in a peaceful way, let there be Croatia, let there be Macedonia, let there be Slovenia, let there be Bosnia. But instead of doing it peacefully, they started to destroy the constitution which dated back to 1974. On the 22nd of December, 1992, deleted Serbs as a constituent people of Yugoslavia, and this is the origin of the evil. The evil had another form, symbols from the Second World War were introduced, and this annoyed people. People were afraid of those symbols because the swastika, and I believe that the Honourable Chamber has that document, so the swastika irritates everybody, not only the Serbs. So that was the second reason. And a third reason was that the nationalist or ethnically-based parties were set up. The HDZ, the SDA, and the SDS. These ethnically-based parties, sewed the seed of discord, who helped those parties, it will be up to history to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can you please switch on the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. We learned from your testimony that Bosanski Brod is situated close, directly, to Croatia. Have you been aware of fugitives coming from Croatia? When did this development start, if there was such a development?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Croatia, on the 4th or on the 5th of May, 1991, a village called Bijelse near Slavonski Brod was attacked. It had a predominant Serb population. The village was surrounded, fenced off, and mined. The Serbs, 87 of them, were taken to various camps. And the Serbs from the village fled the village, and they ran away to Bosnia and Herzegovina because at the time, the war had not started in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That happened, again, on the 15th of July. And this escalated when the barracks were occupied in Slavonski Brod on the 15th of September, 1991, when the barracks were surrounded. That scene, to be seen or to be heard, it was terrible. There were loud speakers all around the barracks. The barracks were surrounded. The few soldiers in there who were Croats, Macedonians, and Muslims, they surrendered immediately. And the rest did not dare do that. There was an armed rebellion in the barracks. The soldiers were captured and they were put on trial in Slavonski Brod. And it is interesting to see the decision of the Croat court in Slavonski Brod. When the officers were tried, the decision says that from the southern banks of the River Sava, not a single bullet was shot which means from the Bosnian side, no single bullet was shot. All that there were already soldiers in Bosanski Brod at that time. So that means that the barracks were captured, and already on the 16th of September, all the Serbian villages on the territory of Bosanski Brod were shelled from Croatia. An engineer was killed. His name was Goranovic. He was killed in the workplace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever seen yourself a mass movement of fugitives, of war fugitives, coming back from Croatia? Did they stay in your town, in your municipality, or did they move through your municipality? And do you know in which direction they headed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the 1991 census, there were about 7.300 Serbs in Bosanski Brod approximately. There were over 2600 Yugoslavs. That means mixed marriages. So if you add up these two figures, you will come up with over 10.000 citizens all together. Around 3500 Serbs crossed from Slavonski Brod, from the Croatian side, to the Bosnian side, to Bosanski Brod. So these were refugees from Croatia. The columns could be seen on the bridge, and the columns were also across the River Sava, in boats, and whatever means there were, people would resort to them in order to save their own life. People fled to Bosnia because they believed that there would be no war in Bosnia, that there couldn't be war in Bosnia because of the multiethnic composition of the population, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. However, we were wrong when we thought that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are awfully sorry that we, the Judges, did not have yet an opportunity to come in our capacity to the territory of Former Yugoslavia. Therefore, my question: Can you give me an estimate about the distance from your hometown to the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Banja Luka, Prijedor, Brod, I can't tell you exactly, but about 160 kilometres approximately. Thereabouts. I can't tell you exactly. I can't give you an approximate figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you yourself ever been in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever met before Dr. Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask, Judge Vassylenko, you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: A couple of them. Witness, can you tell us about ideas or plans to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina between Croatia and Serbia proper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any specific knowledge. But what I read in the printed press, the newspapers and magazines carried a story about a napkin on which Tudjman drew the borders of the future Bosnia. The border was supposed to be along the River Bosnia down to Sarajevo, and then further on to Neum. But this is what the media carried. How correct is that, I don't know. We have not come across any documents indicating any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can we have the mike on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Giving rather extensive answers to one of the questions of the Prosecutor, it seems to me you stated that it is a shame for European Union to support the emergence of a Catholic state in Europe. Maybe I didn't understand you correctly, or if so, I apologise if you stated so. I ask you to explain what did you mean.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, there has been a misunderstanding. I said that a state has been created, and this is extremely misfortunate. Serbs from Croatia were cleansed. They came to Bosnia. From there, they were expelled to Serbia. Their houses were burnt, their property was burned, their apartments, the Serb apartments, were burned. Now, when they are supposed to return, we are returning into Croat or Muslim apartments. I, for one, I am in a Muslim apartment. Mine was burned down and looted. The building still stands, but I don't have the money to repair my apartment. I live in somebody else's apartment. I know I have to leave it, but where am I supposed to go? I'm old. My pension is very low. It's under 200 German marks a month. So now I am faced with a problem. Serbs are returning to Bosnia to their own homes. What about the Serbs who came to Bosnia from Croatia? They now live in somebody else's houses. They do not have access to their own property. And let's understand that for once. If everybody were to return to their place, to their original place, to their property, then this has to apply to Croatia, Slovenia, Macedonia, and to Bosnia-Herzegovina. And only in that way we are going to help each other. It is -- it would be good if we could start communicating as people. This would result in the lowering of tensions, and we will go back to a normal life. Your question, Your Honour, is really good, and I thank you for it. I'm sitting here in front of you, and you can see what I have been reduced to. I haven't seen my granddaughter for 11 years. I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. can't see her. For security reasons, she cannot come to me. She has started school. And this is what is killing me. And it is not just me that have such a case. There's a number of citizens with similar stories. Therefore, when this issue is resolved jointly, then we will also resolve a problem that Europe has. We are not the people who are afraid of work. We work all over Europe, in Germany and the Netherlands and France. We are good workers. We will be able to provide for ourselves. We will be able to live our daily bread. But let's first get to each other. Let's forgive each other our respective sins. Once we do that, everybody will be better off. Europe, the whole world. But we have to work on that. We shouldn't just wait for Europe to give us help, some food packages. And that is why our association has been founded. This is an association which seeks the truth, all of us to tell the truth and that is how we want to help each other and the entire world for that. And believe me when I tell you, vehicles with a checkerboard flag drives from Slavonski Brod to Bosanski Brod, nobody reacts. If a similar thing happened in the reverse direction, if a Serbian symbols were on the car, the cars driving from Bosanski to Slavonski Brod, then we would see it. This is a bad thing for the Balkans. This is a bad thing for Bosnia, which still has a multiethnic composition. I can go to a mosque. I can go to a Catholic church. Because there's only one God. There's only one Christ. There's no one God for Muslims; there's no another God for orthodox religion. There's only one God. And as long as the ethnically based parties have support, the evil will go on. I don't belong to any party. I will never belong to any party ever again. This is evil, and this means no peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't fully understand the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a small association, mostly only this gentleman. So it's very easy to identify him through the association.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So may it be redacted from the transcript, but we know about it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We took the initiative and moved to private session. So this was said in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It was said in private session. So therefore, there's no risk. May I then ask Judge Argibay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I have a question for you. You talk about the ethnically based parties, and that suddenly before the war, the war started, you started seeing different symbols or flags or something that identify with the different parties. Those symbols came up just from one day to the other that you started seeing swastikas or whatever on the walls or you listen to the radio, to the media with propaganda? How did this come out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The internal factor which served to break up Yugoslavia on the media hit the bull's eye in the media. Serbs were called Chetniks. Croats were called Ustasha. Muslims were called mujahedins, and there you go. That's how evil happens. The Second World War in this area resulted in terrible things such was Jasenovac and other places of torture. When these symbols reappeared, they reappeared in Croatia first. They became an integral part of official documents, and that was bad. If you look at video footage from the war, and if you watch it, you will be terrified by all the derogatory words. And this is what people were afraid of, and they started fleeing. And for as long as there are these tensions in place, there will be no peace. And the parliaments, the respective parliaments, support that. And we should tell each other the truth. We should sit at the same table and resolve the matters. I told you about the mass graves. When we wanted to find them, we sat down at the same table, Muslims, Croats, Serbs from Serbia, Serbs from Bosnia, and we said to each other: "Let's be truthful. Let's tell each other. Let's admit to each other where the mass graves are so that the mothers could light a candle on their sons' graves." And then we found out there was a mass grave in Slavonski Brod. That was the major result. So this is a sticking point in the entire case. And when this is finally solved, there will be peace. There will be prosperity for all of us. I apologise. Let me tell you another thing: The greeting "God and Croats," do you know what that means? It means the same thing as if somebody said God and Serbs, God and Muslims. How can one people be identified with God? We are all children of God. You, me. We are all God's children. And what if, for example, a Dutch person said: "The Dutch and the God?" This is what brings fear. This is what instills fear among the people. And if somebody says "I am God's child" why would one person be more valuable than the other because he is a Catholic and I am an Orthodox? And as long as these parties are in power, there will be no peace, people will not be reconciliated. We can raise funds, we can bring people before all sorts of courts, but there will be no real peace until this is resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Defence counsel had some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just short ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness DA, there was a military station in Bosanski Brod, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As of the 3rd of October [as interpreted], 1992, until the beginning of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The transcript says from the 3rd October. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From the 3rd March, 1992, until the 6th October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the army the one who committed misdeeds in Slavonski Brod?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which army you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: HVO, the Croat/Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was the army which was under this military rule?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army which was under the command of this military administration did what they did. They scorched Posavina. They scorched land. All of the religious facilities were brought down, museums, monuments to victims of World War II. Jewish cemeteries, Jewish monuments. All this was destroyed. There are documents, and I believe this Tribunal has them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this military administration issued orders to the army that was under its command, is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the command, the command for Posavina was in Croatia. It was called east Posavina, with the seat in Djakovo and Slavonski Brod, depending on the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Djakovo and Slavonski Brod are towns in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Croatia, neighbouring towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My first question, sir, is do you agree that your testimony is used in other cases, if so requested, under the same conditions? That means under the same protective measures as applicable under your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But just let me add -- yes. But let me add, my story is ten years long. I haven't told you a great many things. But yes, of course, I do agree. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I have to thank you very much for coming here, telling us. I know it's only a very short part of the story you could tell this Tribunal. But I'm quite sure that you heard from, especially from the Defence counsel, why we have to limit in this Tribunal, in this concrete case, our questions to a certain area. And I'm quite sure that under the mandate of this Tribunal, to prosecute all war crimes committed on the territory of Former Yugoslavia since 1991, there will be not only made use of your testimony, but I can't exclude that maybe in future you will be summoned once again when it's a case against the responsible ones responsible for that what happened to you and to your beloved ones. Thank you for coming, and you're excused for today. May I ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. Thank you for listening to me. I am confident -- I profoundly believe that this Court will be fair and just, that they will -- that you will dispense justice whichever side may be responsible for a war crime. I think that everybody should account for what they did. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we proceed with the next witness, may I ask the Defence counsel to proceed in the spirit we discussed yesterday, to concentrate on the core issues. And first of all, not to go one step further and to introduce documents which seems to be not relevant for this concrete case. You have seen that the Chamber will not, in the presence of a witness, discuss the relevance because our judicial terms will not be understood by witnesses. And therefore, please I ask you once more, show the necessary self-restraint when we proceed now with the next witness. But let me first ask, did you receive the requested statements listed in your motion on mistrial?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And finally, only that it not be forgotten, what about the famous page 81? I think it's not necessary to have a new number. It goes under the same number, if the Madam Registrar could assist us. What is the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So the record is clear, this is S235. And the ERN number is 0201-1796.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So it will be numbered S235-81.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for clarification, all documents were already admitted into evidence, and also this page is now admitted as S235-81. It's still from the Prosecutor's case. I don't think that we have other urgent administrative matters before us. Protective measures for the next witness are, once again, pseudonym, which would be DB. And face and voice distortion. And I take it that the testimony will not take longer than 90 minutes as we can read from your summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Hopefully we'll finish by that time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Only that you know, we have to make the break, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. then, at 12.30. May I ask the usher to bring into the courtroom Witness DB. May I ask for an urgent correction of the transcript. On page 30, line 4, it reads: "Fortunately..." Correctly, it has to read "unfortunately." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May we please hear your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated again. And already in the beginning, I have to apologise that we will call you only "Witness" or "Witness DB." This is for your own protection on the request of the Defence. And it's not a sign of impoliteness or uncourtesy. So please understand it's for your own protection. So the floor is for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would like the usher to show the witness a paper with her name so she can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you see your name on this sheet of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence as D39.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. DB.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please speak up a little so that people in the department for interpretation can hear you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we start?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to begin with the 3rd of March, 1992. Will you tell us, where did you live? Who did you live with? And what happened that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I was living with my husband and two daughters in Brod, in our apartment. That is where we lived, and troops of HVO came to our door. They fired shots, entered, searched the flat because allegedly we had the radio station [as interpreted]. Of course they didn't find it because we didn't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, where were your daughters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: My older daughter was in Banja Luka at the university there, and my younger one I sent to Belgrade -- no, sorry, to Novi Sad, to her aunt.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you just, after I've asked you a question, will you please wait a moment so that my question could be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And why did you send your daughter to her aunt in Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Well, I had begun to be afraid of the Croatian troops. They had come to search our house, and they were armed when they came to our place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And your older daughter, you say, was at university in Banja Luka. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And after the 3rd of March, 1992, could you move freely around Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: No, I could not. I could not move around.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When and how did you leave your apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't easy to go out. It was always difficult because they always followed closely, where we moved around, what we did. So we did not really dare move about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did your husband leave the apartment following the 3rd of March?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: No, he did not. But my husband had already by that time taken in. He was arrested. He was taken under custody to where they kept those prisoners in camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, your mother lived in Sijekovac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened in Sijekovac on the 26th of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I heard about the slaughter in Sijekovac because my school fellow called Nedo and his men committed a slaughter there. They broke into a small street called Milosevic Sokak and they just slew everybody. They slaughtered everybody. I did not see, that but I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened on Serb Easter in Lijeske, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, I do. As announced that the Serb Easter would be bloody. All Serb villages were taken by Croatian troops at the time, and they started putting houses on fire, killing everybody they happened to come across.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Prior to the 11th of September, 1992, how many times did the Croatian military forces take in your husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Three times before the 11th of September. Three times they took him in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Until the 11th of September, or the 11th of November?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: September.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And he would be detained for how long on those three occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Well, between 10 and 15 days, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All together, 10, 15, or every time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Every time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened on the 11th of September, 1992, to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: They came and took away both me and my husband and put us in camps. He was put with men, and me with other women.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After you were detained, what happened to you then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
