utterances.text: When I entered -- as I entered there, one of those HVO soldiers, he had the mark of the 108th unit. He took me into a room. He snatched away my handbag and told me to undress. Because we were ashamed to do that, he started undressing me. And he hit me somewhere here. And I fell as he hit me. I just fell down. And then he said: "Lie down so that we can make a little Ustasha." And I had -- I could not fight any more. And that is how it went on day in day out, night after night evermore. Of these rapes, it was the worst when they took me to the military positions, that is where they hold positions. That is when I felt the worst because that is when they raped me there so 11 through the night, and that is how they just queued for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you raped once a week, once a fortnight, every day, how often was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Every night. They did not skip a single night for the duration of my stay there. They did not spare me a single night. By day, I had to work. And by night, rapes, torture.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what about the men who were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Let me tell you another thing that they did to me and that I found very difficult, too. I don't really know how to tell you that. They forced me to kneel in front of them, and they would put their penis in my mouth. And of course they either hold you by your hair or they kick you if you try to spit it out. And then they do it in your mouth. And I have to hide it somehow. I dare not spit it out, and I have to try to spit it out into my T-shirt to hide that I am doing that. But you were asking me about men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since we are back to this subject, are you the only one who was raped, or were other women raped, too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: We were all raped, all the women that were there. We were all raped. But somehow, I was used most. I don't really know why. Well, I was younger than those other women. I was younger.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned also a Muslim woman. Could you tell us what happened to her.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, [redacted]. She is a Muslim. She was also detained in the camp. We were together. And she was accused -- she was accused because allegedly her brother's son was in the army, and she was accused because of that. She was also tortured and raped, and she was also taken to the frontline except that they took me to one side of the village, and they took her to another side, to Kricanovo which is another village adjacent to -- adjoining Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I'm sorry, Your Honour. Are we in open session or private session, and if we are in open session, if possible we would like to redact this name of this other victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see no objections. Please redact the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was my mistake, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around the 25th of September, 1992, were you transferred somewhere, and where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: From the stadium to the secondary school in Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did the same practice continue there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes. The routine was the same. It was just the same, same Croatian troops. It was all the same. We were the same except that the camp was different. And they brought another woman there. [redacted] [redacted], who was from Teslic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the witness to refrain from quoting names because we don't want to endanger these persons. So may the name please be redacted from the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened with that woman, but don't mention her name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I won't. She was also tortured. She was raped, and on one night, which I will never forget, we couldn't do anything. We were not allowed to do anything. We could just hear to her screams. And I can't even begin to describe the screams that we heard. And during the night, I don't know how late it was, they just opened the door and threw her into our room where we were. And when we saw her, we just dragged her to the mattress where she lie down. In the morning, we couldn't recognise her. She didn't have a single hair on her head, and she was all burnt. Her bottom was burnt most of all. Then her elbows, both of her elbows. Her knees. Every joint was -- on her body was burnt. Later on, I went to that room where they had tortured her, and I saw a white electrical stove with two plates. And they obviously put her on that little electrical stove and burned her, electrical heater. And she was beaten black and blue, and the hair was there. Later on when I cleaned the room, I saw her hair. And from then onwards, she was bedridden. We served upon her, and she was incontinent. And she couldn't tell us anything. She didn't know a thing about anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you remained in the secondary school until when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Until the 6th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you taken from there? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: They made us run across the bridge to Slavonski Brod. And since that woman, she couldn't walk, they put her in a car and transported her on to the Croatian side. And then we took her and dragged her. We had to run. We had to flee. And we couldn't drag her, and there was a trench there. She fell into it. She asked for some water, for a drink of water. And we were not allowed to give her any water. They made us run all the time. She fell down, and two men from the Croatian army who ordered us to move on, they shot at her. They had rifles, and they shot at her. And that's where she remained, lying down on the ground, and the rest of us, we continued running.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why were you transported on the 6th of October, 1992, from Bosanski to Slavonski Brod?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: We didn't know. Nobody told us anything. The Serbian army came and liberated Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And where were you transported on the same night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: We didn't know where we were going. They put us on lorries, and they transported us to Orasje, to the camp there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to you in that camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Everything was the same, rapes, torture. The men were forced to work. In the evening, they would be beaten. They would be kicked. And we all had to be in one room, both the men and the women. We were all there together in Orasje, and we could see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of a group known as "fire horses" in Orasje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes. He is -- he was a fire horse. He was the main person there. I don't know whether I'm supposed to mention his name at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can mention his name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: His name was Petar, Pero.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was his role in Orasje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: He was the main person in Orasje. I don't know what his rank was. I don't know what the ranks of the Croatian soldiers were, but he was the one who was beating our men the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he also run the camp in Orasje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Until when did you stay in Orasje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I stayed there until the 24th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how did your confinement stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: What do you mean by "stop"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of November, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: The two of us, two women, were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was anybody else supposed to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, some of our men were also supposed to be exchanged, but none of them were actually exchanged. Only the two of us, the two women.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were incarcerated, did any representatives of the international community come to register you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes. They came while we were in Brod. They came on several occasions, but then they would hide us. They would take the women away. The men would stay behind. They would dig trenches. And the women would be taken away and wait until the end of the visit. So they would mostly hide us women from the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, the representatives of the international community managed to register you in Orasje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, they did register us in Orasje when they came there. That's where they first registered us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And after that, you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes. The two of us, me and another woman were sent to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was your husband in the same camps as you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, he was. And later on, when I left to be exchanged, he was transferred to another camp in -- somewhere in Herzegovina. I forgot the name of that camp. I can't remember the name of that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he transferred to Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, Ljubuski, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long was your husband incarcerated all together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: 11 months he was incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you suffer any consequences of all that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes. Firstly, my marriage is now over. He left. He knew of all my sufferings. I knew of all of his, and we couldn't understand each other obviously. And the consequences that I personally suffer, the medical consequences, that is, I live on tablets. I can't go to sleep without tablets. I'm afraid every time when somebody knocks on my door. To this very day, I'm afraid, and I start shaking all over. I have gynaecological problems also. And two months ago, I had something for which I had to undergo a surgery. So I still suffer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Can you please remain in your seat. Maybe my learned friend from the Prosecution and the Honourable Judges will have some questions to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Madam, thank you for coming, and for your courage in testifying. We all can understand how very difficult it is, and painful. You talked that the same thing or many of the same things that happened to you happened to other women. Can you tell us, coming from Bosnia, do you think for many women it's impossible for them to tell other people about the suffering, and particularly about the sexual crimes against them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, it is impossible. I am ashamed to tell you all this. I'm sure they must be, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, Madam, you should be proud for your courage and not ashamed. You mentioned being in several different camps with women. And it sounds, if I'm correct, that these crimes happened in every camp --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: -- in all of these camps during the war where you were held by soldiers, sexual crimes happened. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you think those people who set up these camps and put women in these camps run by soldiers should have been aware of the risk they put those women in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: They should have been aware. I believe they should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mention that those running the camps tried to hide your presence, the presence of women, from the international community. And actually you're not the first witness to talk about the Croatian army hiding women held in camps from the international community and the international press. Did you find in your experience that there were deliberate efforts by the authorities to keep your presence, the presence of women, in camps hidden?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes. They made an effort to hide us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And in fact, once the International Red Cross was able to register you, it led eventually to your release. So there was some protection, you felt some protection, from the International Red Cross registering you and coming to the camp. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you think of any reason why authorities would keep the International Red Cross away from camps and keep camps hidden, except to conceal crimes that they know were occurring in those camps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry. Do you think that the authorities tried to keep the camps hidden or keep the presence of women and those camps hidden in order to conceal the crimes that they knew were going on in the camps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They knew, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Madam, thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I do believe that your testimony speaks for itself. And the Judges, therefore, refrain from asking any additional questions. May I only ask you, do you agree that in case it will be necessary that your testimony is used as well in other cases against alleged offenders responsible for the crimes you described us this day, under the same conditions? This means under the protective measures granted to you in this testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, because I have been through all this. This is the truth. And I have told you nothing else but the truth of the things that I have been through. This is what I've told you today, Your Honours. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have to thank you for your courageous testimony. We all are aware how difficult it is for you, not only to come here, but to reopen the wounds coming back to that what you suffered at that period in time. And be assured that this Tribunal in its entirety will do all the necessary to bring those to justice being responsible for the crimes committed. Thank you and have a safe return. May I ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 12.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we continue with the next witness. The same protective measures, and pseudonym would be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please turn the microphone on, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- DC. And we have face and voice distortion. May I ask the usher to bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you to give the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I supposed to read this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And first of all, my apologies that we don't address you with your full name. It's a protective measure requested by the Defence, so it has nothing to do with impoliteness. It's just to protect you when we call you either "witness" or "Witness DC." Thank you for this understanding. And the floor is for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would first like --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- so the witness can confirm that her name is on this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be Exhibit D40. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. DC.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please make a break after my question so that the interpreters can do their job properly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll start by asking you questions about the 3rd of March, 1992. Do you remember that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you remember about that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: On the 3rd of March, 1992 the Croat and Muslim army entered Tulek. This is the periphery of Bosanski Brod. It was heavily armed. It had armoured personnel carriers. It was around 5.00 in the afternoon. There was a lot of shooting going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you live after the 3rd of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: The 3rd of March, it was terrible. I was surprised because my neighbours who lived next to my house was among the Croat houses, and we had lived very well together. And I was really surprised to see them coming out of their houses armed, as if they had all known about what would happen, as if they had been prepared. This is what surprised me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you allowed to move freely around Bosanski Brod at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: It was really bad. When the Croat and Muslim forces went to the frontline, then I could move around. Then I could find some food, so I was able to eat. It was almost like a house prison for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why were you not able to move around Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Because of the Croat army and because of the Muslim army. They forbade us to move freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was celebrated on the 11th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: On the 11th of May, 1992, the celebration was about them capturing Brod. They were singing songs, and they were shouting, saying "Thank God Brod is ours, Brod is Croat."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So that means that the Croat forces captured the entire municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Exactly, just the way you've put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to you on the 7th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: On the 7th of July, 1992, I was having lunch in my house, the little food that I had. At that time, two armed military policemen came and told me that they were taking me to the stadium in Bosanski Brod. I asked them why. They said we don't know. Blazina Kraljevic, Ferdo, ordered us to bring us in, and if we don't do that, it will be held against us. So what could I do? Together with my husband, I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you taken? What was that place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: On the 7th of July, 1992, I was taken to the stadium in Bosanski Brod, and this is where we were imprisoned. My husband was with the men, and I was with the women. So they separated us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that a regular prison? Was that a prison before the war or --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Before the war, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "prison" --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was a camp, not a prison. We were taken to a camp. I apologise. I'm a bit confused. We were taken to a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you keep -- did they keep you together with your husband or did they separate you from each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: They separated us from each other. My husband was taken to the male camp, and I was taken to the female camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened to you three or four days later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Four days after that, they had bunkbeds on the stadium, and this is where they started ill treating me, harassing me. And I heard them telling each other that they would massacre me, and they showed me how the weapons looked like with which they would massacre me. They told me we would massacre you and we would throw your clothes into the Sava. It was a terrible shock for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that the only thing that happened to you in that camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: No. There were other things. They raped women. There were ten of us in that room in the camp. Around 5.00 in the evening, they would start taking us out, and this lasted until 5.00 in the morning. So it went on night in, night out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many times were you taken out in one night, on average?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Two times, three times maybe. Both me and the other ten women who were in that room in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you allowed to move freely around the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you allowed to move freely around the camp or were you locked up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: We were always locked up. I was locked up. Only when they raped us, then they would unlock the door, and they all had the key. And when they were supposed to bring us food, only one of them would have the key. But when they were supposed to rape us, then they would all have the key. How come they all had the key at the time when they were supposed to rape us? I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your incarceration, did you lose any weight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. 10, 15, or maybe even 20 kilos I lost. I was afraid. There was not enough food. For all these reasons, I lost weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the military unit that arrested you on the 7th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: I was arrested by Nermin from Slavonski Brod. That was his name. And the other guy, he was from Sijekovac, but I don't know his name. They were the ones who took me to the camp in Bosanski Brod at the stadium in Bosanski Brod. They took both me and my husband together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the unit that they belonged to? Were they the army, the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: As far as I knew, they were the HVO, the Croat/Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe the event which took place in July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: In July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you said that a lot of troops came.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Please remind me, and I'll tell you everything. One night, a lot of troops came and lined the ten of us up in that room. And they raped us there and then. And the guy from Sijekovac who arrested me and whose name I don't know, he told me that I was good. And I told him: "Shame on you. I could be your mother." Then he slapped me. I screamed. And from then on, I'm hard of hearing in my left ear. And then Manda from Korac, she shouted: "Get out. It's enough." When I started screaming, and then they left the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you transferred on the 21st of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: On the 21st of August, 1992, I was transferred to Tulek. That was a local commune consisting of all the three ethnic backgrounds, and this is where the Croat/Muslim army was. This is where they rallied, and this is where they committed genocide in Bosanski Brod. And I was transferred to Tulek, in the warehouse of the Belgrade department store. That's where I spent five days. And after five days, we were taken to Slavonski Brod and Slavonska Pozega in a personnel armoured carrier. And they asked us why we were incarcerated. And I told them I really don't know. It's not me who started the war. I believe I'm incarcerated because I'm a Serb from Slavonska Pozega. And then they took us back to Tulek, and from there we were exchanged in Dragalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was your husband incarcerated in the same camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes, my husband remained in the warehouse of the department store when I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to him when he remained there in the warehouse of the Belgrade department store after you had left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. My husband was returned to the prison at the stadium, to the military prison at the stadium. And on that night, they beat up our men. And he was unconscious. And a man who was with him in the camp, the man was from Prnjavor, and I went to visit him in Prnjavor, he told me that they poured water over him, and he came to. Then a soldier came and hit him on the head with a bottle. And he started bleeding behind the left ear. And then from then on, he didn't give a sign of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And your husband was killed that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes, the 30th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: 1992. The 30th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before he came to the camp, was your husband a healthy man or was he suffering from something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: My husband had a brain tumor, and he had had an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we go on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were detained at the stadium, did you hear about how men were beaten next door?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes. I could hear the screams of my husband right next door to the place where I was. When he cried out, Oh, my God, I'll remember when this war happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, there was no more fighting in the Bosanski Brod Municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Which time do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: July and August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: What do you mean there was no fighting? Of course there was, until Brod fell into the Serb hands on the 6th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there any gunfire in relation to the fighting in July and August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes, there was gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned bags and the rustling of those bags. It reminded you of something.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't sleeping well because I was so traumatized, and I was suffering from nightmares so I couldn't really sleep. And I could hear them being hit and interrogated, and all of a sudden I heard a shot from a firearm. And I could hear the rustling of plastic bags and how they were being taken into a car, and taken away to where mass graves were found behind -- on the other side of the Sava in Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they hide you in the kayak club and why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: In August 1992, a soldier came and fired a pistol into the door lock of the room that we were kept locked in and told us: "Get ready, you're going." And I asked where? And he refused to answer. Allegedly, that we looked fine and that they are Croats and Muslims, and as inmates they looked worse than we did. But that wasn't it. They were hiding us from UNPROFOR to avoid having us registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And from the kayak club, did they take you back to the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Three days later. And when we got to that room, we left it clean behind. But when we returned, it looked like nothing that room. It looked better -- I mean, places where livestock are kept looked better. It wasn't fit for human residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you know why was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: There were bloodstains. It was dirty. It was horrible. Ten of us put our sleeves up and cleaned it. What went on there, I do not know. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. But judging by the filth, obviously nothing good happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And apart from beating up men in the camp, did they also have to do certain chores?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes, they took them to dig trenches. The Muslim military police took men because one was presumably building a house, so -- and how he built during a war, how could he build a house when there was a war on? So they were taken there. In the evening, they beat them. And we suffered twice because we suffered our own pain, and we suffered the pain of the men because the bathrooms were adjoining, so one could hear everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was Indira Vrbanjac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Indira Vrbanjac was at the stadium in Bosanski Brod. She was admitting us into the camp, and she took our names down. And she forced Serbs to rape us. And that Serb whom she tried to make to rape me, he said: "Madam, you can't do it. I mean, that's now how things can happen." And Hazba Nukic from Kobasi, he [as interpreted] forced him to sit into a Serb's lap and to press her breasts, and he refused to do that. And then she approached that Serb, this Indira Vrbanjac, and told him and Hazba told me about that after she came back, we did not really talk, but in that room we were kept, we only whispered into each other's ears because we were afraid that perhaps the room might be bugged. And well, if you refused to press her breasts, then I'll start kicking you. So what else this poor sap could do. He was forced to start doing that. And her husband started screaming, he could not stand any more. That is Hazba Nukic. And then Indira Vrbanjac said: "That's enough. You don't have to do it any longer."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is Hazba's last name Nukic, N-u-k-i-c?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: That's right, Nukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what is her ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: She is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And Indira Vrbanjac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Indira Vrbanjac is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Indira Vrbanjac participate in organising other tortures of prisoners at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose so, if she did this to Hazba Nukic who personally told me about it, then I don't think she went on doing that because she was nationally minded. Indira Vrbanjac was married to a Muslim. And when a Muslim heard how she mistreated Serbs, he left her and then she remarried and married a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whilst your husband was alive, how often did they beat him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: When they took us to the kayaking club next to the Sava, I was with my husband then, and he told me that he had been beaten three or four times a day. And he had to wash cars, and they made him wash the same car ten times over and beat him in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you were incarcerated, you were detained, until the 26th of August, 1992, and then you were exchanged. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes. I was exchanged -- I was taken to the camp on the 7th of July, 1992, and I was exchanged on the 26th of August, 1992 at Dragalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions. But please stay here because perhaps the Prosecutor and Their Honours might have questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour. I don't have any questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Argibay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I'll try to be as clear as possible. But I remember you said at the beginning of your testimony that you were forbidden by the Croat army and the Muslim army to move around the town. How were you forbidden? Did they come and tell you you can't do this, or was an announcement made, or was it physically impeding you to go around? Can you answer that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: I can, yes. My neighbours said the same thing. "Don't move around." And the military said the same thing. "You may not move around, and you may not stop in groups of Serbs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Well, thank you. And I have another one. You talked in that same paragraph, I mean, of the Croat army and the Muslim army. Were there two separate armies, and can you -- if it was two separate armies, can you tell me what was the difference between one and the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that. All I heard was that it was the Croat and Muslim troops, the HVO. And I was in the military police prison at the stadium in Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony. May I, in addition, ask you whether you are --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- whether you agree that your testimony, if necessary, can be used in other trials as to the fact that this Tribunal is mandated to prosecute all persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law committed in the territory of the Former Yugoslavia since 1991. That means also those ones responsible for the crimes committed against you and your beloved ones. Do you agree that under the same circumstances, we'll say the same protective measures, your testimony can be used in other cases as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Well, what am I to answer? This was difficult for me, and I'd rather not testify again because I'm still afraid. I dare not go to Slavonski Brod. I dare not move around. And I barely managed to do this. But I came to tell you about my ordeal, about what they did to me and my husband.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We all are extremely grateful that you decided to come and that you were indeed courageous to testify here about that what happened to you. The question is, our rules provide for the possibility that your testimony as you can see it on your computer, this can be used in other cases in order to avoid that you have to come twice to The Hague. Therefore my question, do you agree that this document is used in other cases as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: I'm a very traumatized woman. I somehow managed to go through this, but I'd rather not go any further. I apologise, but I really can't go any further because this is, again, a traumatic experience, and I'm badly shattered already. I cannot bear to talk about this any more about this because it has been 11 years and I want these wounds to heal rather than have them opened over and over again. And may this not happen again ever again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may assist, Your Honour, maybe it will be easier in our language. [Interpretation] His Honour is asking you whether you accept that the record that was made of your testimony be used in another case with the same kind of protection here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean in another case? You want me to come here again here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course it may be used. I'm sorry, I didn't understand. Of course, it may be used. Why not use it again, because what I went through, I'm not ashamed of that. And I've sworn that I will tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It remains only for us to thank you for your testimony, and at least to try to overcome all this what has happened to you. We know it's extremely difficult. But once again, thank you. And have a safe return back to your home country and hometown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You're excused for today. And may I ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. All the best to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you are prepared for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm prepared but the witness is not Your Honour because we counted that the Prosecution might have some questions and you too so the next witness is not here, Your Honour. And actually, asked for him yesterday, but because of the long testimony this morning of the first witness, I advised the victims and witness unit not to bring him at the end of this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That means that we will proceed tomorrow with the three remaining witnesses being already in The Hague. There was scheduled another 65 ter (i) meeting of one afternoon in the week. I don't see, after having had the meeting yesterday, any necessity. Do the parties agree, or is there any need for having such a 65 ter (i) conference once again this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't see any need, and we thank you that we had that meeting outside of the open court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We don't see a need for a meeting, but we reiterate that we're waiting for a witness list that's complete with the full names and diacritics of the witnesses and a summary of what the witnesses will testify to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask whether or not we can expect a written submission by the Prosecution as regards the remaining part of the motion on mistrial, that is, point (a).

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we did not plan to file anything written because -- we would, if Your Honours believe it would be helpful. We made our position clear that the Defence has failed to specify how any of the information that they did receive that the Prosecution has acknowledged they should have received sooner, but how, if they had received this information sooner, their cross-examination would have been any different for any of the witnesses. I think the information that was provided in those summaries went to issues that the Defence cross-examined the witnesses on the first day of the trial. So we do not believe that any witness's testimony should be stricken or that the cross-examination would have been any different. If the Defence believes that it would be, we have offered to bring the witness back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Therefore, you make reference to the transcript of yesterday only where I think indeed you gave sufficient reason. As regards the other summaries, after having seen the entire statements at that time, I have to ask the Defence once again, maybe after consultation with the accused in person, is it your position that, having had the possibility now to review these documents, that you insist on a decision on the remaining point (a) of your motion bearing in mind that no doubt, there is a possibility either to resummon or to summon the witness? And therefore, it might be the outcome that no prejudice is the result from this omission of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I have to say, but I didn't have time to go through the statements, full statements, we received yesterday Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. evening because we finished our meeting at 6.00, and then I stayed with the witnesses until 11.00 last night speaking with them. So I really didn't have time to go through the complete statements, and I hope that I will be able to do it the day after tomorrow because tomorrow I have to be -- tonight I have to be with the witnesses again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But today, we'll provide by the end of the day, we'll provide the Prosecution with a more detailed proffer, and with the properly written names of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you agree that we wait with our decision until we have got a final answer on our question as regards the motion for mistrial, maybe after discussing this issue with your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then finally, as agreed, we will hear the three remaining witnesses tomorrow. And then you will let us know what is your intention whom to summon the three remaining days in December. Also for the transcript, it has to be fixed that there is not only the Monday and Tuesday, but also the Wednesday available for the Defence as to the fact that the plenary of the Judges will take place only on Thursday and Friday. So therefore, as agreed, we expect your answer on Thursday as well as regards these -- the one or two witnesses to be heard on these three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Hopefully we'll be able to bring more witnesses for these three days, Your Honour. But we'll inform you in any case until Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Also, only for the purposes of the transcript, the Defence is aware of the fact that in case they shouldn't have the relevant testimonies available for these three days, the Trial Chamber will make use of their rights under Rule 85 V. This is to summon witnesses ex officio.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We are aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Any additional comments or administrative matters to be addressed today?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have anything else, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This concludes today's hearing. The trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: at 1.27 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 20th day of November, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
